newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss expect concept for gold-based fund by autumn.
newsitem.headline: Swiss expect concept for gold-based fund by autumn.

text.p: The Swiss government will this year unveil a detailed plan for its proposed seven billion Swiss franc foundation that would use gold sales to fund humanitarian aid projects, the finance ministry said on Thursday.

"The finance minister will present the cabinet by autumn the concept for the foundation's activities and its management of assets based on preparatory work," it said in a statement, adding a wide range of people would help draw up the plan.

President Arnold Koller last month proposed creating the Swiss Solidarity Foundation that would distribute around 350 million Swiss francs each year at home and abroad to victims of poverty, catastrophes and human rights abuses.

The money represents interest on investments Switzerland can make by revaluing its official gold reserves and selling part of them gradually over 10 years. The central bank now values its gold at 12 billion francs, less than a third of its market value.
Revaluation would boost gold reserves to 26 billion francs, still only around 60 percent of its market value. The foundation would get half of the 14 billion in revaluation profits to invest.
"A condition is that the foundation will work exclusively with proceeds from managing a part of revalued gold reserves that are not needed for gold or currency policy," it said.
"The capital it gets, in whatever form, will not be used up and remains public property," it added. "Special attention must be paid to concerns about currency and inflation policy."
Finance Ministry director Ulrich Gygi will head the interdepartmental group that is overseeing the planning process for Finance Minister Kaspar Villiger.
Four separate committees will look into how to spend the money, asset management, legal aspects and communications.
Ulrich Bremi, a businessman and former president of the lower house of parliament, chairs the group examining how best to raise and invest the proceeds.
Hermann Fehr, health and welfare director for the canton of Berne, will head the panel examining who should get the money and how it can be distributed in an efficient way.

Opponents have blasted the plan as a misguided giveaway of national wealth to appease critics who accuse Switzerland of cynically profiting from World War Two. They have urged Swiss voters to block the idea in a referendum next year.

Koller has said he is confident voters will back the plan, but that approval hinged on convincing Swiss that the foundation was part of the country's humanitarian tradition and that money would be spent wisely.

Opinion polls taken immediately after Koller made the surprise move showed most Swiss backed the plan, but politicial analysts have questioned whether this will still be the case when it comes up for a vote next year.
